paras: The killing of Stephen Anthony was the fatal shooting of a 60-year-old Wallingford, Connecticut, man by his son-in-law, Solon G. Jenkins, at the door of Anthony's home on the evening of 15 November 1888. A wire report carried in western papers said that "angry citizens" threatened to lynch Jenkins after his arrest, though Connecticut papers made no mention of a crowd. Jenkins was bound over for trial and hanged himself in the New Haven County Jail on 20 December 1888.

Jenkins, a tinner by trade, had once kept a stove store in Wallingford, but according to the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier he began to drink heavily and was closed up by the sheriff. His wife, Anthony's daughter, had left him, and Anthony had given her and their three daughters a home and refused Jenkins admission to the house. At the hearing, members of the Anthony family testified that the women of the house lived in fear of him and had arranged a tin-horn signal to summon neighboring sons, and that a threatening unsigned postal card in his handwriting had arrived that morning.

On 15 November Jenkins took a train from New Haven, where he boarded, and told a fellow passenger, Henry Allen, that he would shoot Anthony if refused entry, showing him a revolver. After waiting near the house, he fired when Anthony opened the rear door about 6 o'clock, killing him almost instantly. First reports said the bullet entered the nostril, but the coroner found after the post-mortem that it had entered the right shoulder and passed through both lungs.

Anthony's son overpowered Jenkins, bound him with ropes and delivered him to Officer Reilly, who found a knife and a revolver with two empty chambers on him. In the lockup Jenkins claimed that Anthony had shot first; the Waterbury Evening Democrat thought a wound behind his ear was probably self-inflicted, and the New Haven paper said he had tried to take his own life. A wire brief dated the next day added that he had threatened the rest of the family with death and that "the angry citizens threaten to lynch him."

On 16 November Judge Hubbard of the Borough court bound Jenkins over to the Superior Court, and he was lodged in the New Haven county jail. In court he accused his wife of trying to poison him and of infidelity, charges she denied. Before any trial, Jenkins hanged himself in his cell on 20 December with a towel and his suspenders, leaving notes that confessed the killing and said he died to save the state expense. He was buried in Westville cemetery with no friends or relatives present.

Outside Connecticut the case ran as a one-paragraph wire item under headlines blaming drink, such as "Ruined by Drink" in Astoria, "Rum's Ruin" in Los Angeles and "A Drunken Fiend" elsewhere. The same brief appeared in Seattle, Salt Lake City, Sacramento and Nevada on 17 November and in Oregon a week later. The Butte Semi-Weekly Miner headed its copy "He Deserved Lynching" and gave the accused's name as "Col. N. Jenkins."

Connecticut papers treated the case as a domestic murder: the Waterbury Evening Democrat called it "simply a brutal homicide," and the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier followed the testimony under headlines such as "Jenkins the Murderer." None of these local reports of the arrest, the hearing or the suicide mentions a crowd or a threat of lynching, which appears only in the wire version. No paper stated the race of anyone involved.

The Tribune placed the shooting on "the morning of November 15," while the local papers, writing the next day, put it about 6 o'clock in the evening. The accused's middle initial and name also vary, from "Solon G." in most reports to "Solon S." in Waterbury, "Solon Calthoun" in the Tribune and "Col. N." in Butte.

reader.title: Killing of Stephen Anthony
bases: The only collective-violence element is the wire report that angry citizens threatened to lynch Jenkins after he shot his father-in-law (A2, A11); no one was killed by a crowd, and the local papers describe an individual homicide followed by a court hearing (A1, A3).

No one was killed by a group: Stephen Anthony was shot by one man, Jenkins, and Jenkins himself was held, bound over and later died by suicide in jail (A1, A3, A15). The only report of a crowd is a one-line wire claim that 'angry citizens' threatened to lynch him (A2), which no local paper repeats.

The killing, arrest and committal are reported independently by the wire brief and by Waterbury and New Haven papers (A1, A2, A3), but the lynching threat rests on the wire brief alone and is absent from every local account (A1, A3, A10).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A drink-ruined former merchant shot his father-in-law, threatened the rest of the family with death, was locked up, and angry citizens threatened to lynch him.

accounts.label: Local papers
accounts.gist: Jenkins, estranged from his wife and barred from seeing his children, shot Anthony at the rear door after telling a fellow passenger he would; Anthony's son bound him and handed him to an officer; he was bound over to the Superior Court. No crowd is mentioned.

accounts.label: Jenkins's claim
accounts.gist: In the lockup Jenkins said Anthony shot him first and he fired in self-defense; in court he accused his wife of trying to poison him and of infidelity.

framing.detail: Western papers ran the same brief under drink headlines such as 'Rum's Ruin', 'Crazed With Drink' and 'A Drunken Fiend'.
The Butte Semi-Weekly Miner headed the wire brief 'He Deserved Lynching'.
The New Haven and Waterbury papers called it a 'brutal homicide' and a premeditated murder and followed the court case, with no mention of lynching.

conflicts.note: The local New Haven paper uses Solon G. Jenkins throughout; 'Col. N. Jenkins' appears only in one reprint of the wire.
